title: Network Models
description: Network models define how communication happens between devices by dividing networking tasks into layers. The OSI and TCP/IP models are the most important architectural models used to understand computer networks.

topics.title: Network Layered Architecture
topics.description: Understanding why networking uses layered models and how these layers simplify communication design.

subtopics.title: Why Layered Network Architecture is Needed
subtopics.theory: Networking systems are extremely complex because they involve many tasks such as data transmission, routing, error control, and application communication. To manage this complexity, networking is divided into multiple layers where each layer performs a specific function. Each layer communicates with the layer above and below it using well-defined interfaces. This layered approach simplifies network design, allows interoperability between different vendors, and enables easier troubleshooting and upgrades.

subtopics.title: Encapsulation in Networking
subtopics.theory: Encapsulation is the process of wrapping data with protocol information at each layer of the network model before transmission. When an application sends data, the application layer passes it to the transport layer where headers such as port numbers are added. The network layer then adds IP addressing information. The data link layer adds MAC addresses and frame information. Finally the physical layer transmits the bits over the medium. At the receiver side this process is reversed and called decapsulation.

topics.title: OSI Model
topics.description: The OSI model is a conceptual framework developed by ISO that divides networking into seven layers.

subtopics.title: Overview of OSI Model
subtopics.theory: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model was developed by the International Organization for Standardization to standardize communication between different computer systems. It divides networking functions into seven layers where each layer performs a specific role in data communication. These layers help engineers understand how data flows across networks and how protocols interact.

subtopics.title: Physical Layer (Layer 1)
subtopics.theory: The physical layer is responsible for transmitting raw bits over a physical communication medium such as copper cables, fiber optics, or wireless signals. It defines electrical signals, voltage levels, transmission speed, connectors, and cable types. Devices operating at this layer include hubs, repeaters, and network cables.

subtopics.title: Data Link Layer (Layer 2)
subtopics.theory: The data link layer ensures reliable communication between directly connected devices. It converts raw bits from the physical layer into frames and handles error detection using mechanisms such as CRC. It also manages MAC addressing and controls access to the transmission medium. Devices such as switches and network interface cards operate at this layer.

subtopics.title: Network Layer (Layer 3)
subtopics.theory: The network layer is responsible for routing packets from the source device to the destination device across multiple networks. It determines the best path for data transmission using routing algorithms. Logical addressing such as IP addresses is used at this layer. Routers operate primarily at this layer.

subtopics.title: Transport Layer (Layer 4)
subtopics.theory: The transport layer provides end-to-end communication between applications running on different devices. It ensures reliable data transfer using mechanisms like acknowledgments, sequencing, retransmission, and flow control. Two important protocols operating at this layer are TCP and UDP.

subtopics.title: Session Layer (Layer 5)
subtopics.theory: The session layer manages communication sessions between applications. It establishes, maintains, and terminates connections between two communicating systems. It also provides synchronization and checkpoint mechanisms during long data transfers.

subtopics.title: Presentation Layer (Layer 6)
subtopics.theory: The presentation layer is responsible for data translation, encryption, and compression. It ensures that data sent by the application layer of one system can be correctly interpreted by the application layer of another system. Examples include SSL/TLS encryption and data format conversions.

subtopics.title: Application Layer (Layer 7)
subtopics.theory: The application layer is the top layer of the OSI model and provides network services directly to end-user applications. Protocols such as HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS, and Telnet operate at this layer. It allows applications like browsers, email clients, and file transfer systems to communicate over the network.

topics.title: TCP/IP Model
topics.description: The TCP/IP model is the practical networking model used on the internet.

subtopics.title: Overview of TCP/IP Model
subtopics.theory: The TCP/IP model is the architecture used by the Internet and was developed by DARPA. Unlike the OSI model which has seven layers, the TCP/IP model consists of four layers. These layers are Application, Transport, Internet, and Network Access. It is more practical and directly implemented in real networking systems.

subtopics.title: Application Layer
subtopics.theory: The application layer in TCP/IP combines the functions of the OSI application, presentation, and session layers. It provides services such as web communication, email transmission, and file transfer. Common protocols include HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, DNS, and SSH.

subtopics.title: Transport Layer
subtopics.theory: The transport layer ensures end-to-end communication between hosts. It uses protocols like TCP and UDP. TCP provides reliable communication using acknowledgments and retransmissions while UDP provides faster but unreliable communication.

subtopics.title: Internet Layer
subtopics.theory: The internet layer is responsible for logical addressing and packet routing. It determines how packets travel across multiple networks to reach the destination. The most important protocol at this layer is IP (Internet Protocol). Other supporting protocols include ICMP and ARP.

subtopics.title: Network Access Layer
subtopics.theory: The network access layer handles communication between the host and the physical network. It includes protocols and hardware used for transmitting data over the physical medium. Technologies such as Ethernet and Wi-Fi operate at this layer.

topics.title: OSI vs TCP/IP Comparison
topics.description: Understanding the differences between the OSI and TCP/IP networking models.

subtopics.title: Key Differences Between OSI and TCP/IP
subtopics.theory: The OSI model has seven layers while the TCP/IP model has four layers. OSI is mainly a conceptual reference model used for understanding networking while TCP/IP is a practical implementation used in real networks. In the OSI model, session and presentation layers are separate while TCP/IP merges them into the application layer. OSI strictly separates services, interfaces, and protocols whereas TCP/IP focuses more on protocol implementation.

subtopics.title: Why TCP/IP Became the Standard
subtopics.theory: TCP/IP became the standard networking architecture because it was implemented earlier and used by the ARPANET and later the Internet. It was simpler, more flexible, and widely adopted by operating systems and networking equipment. As the internet expanded globally, TCP/IP became the universal protocol suite for networking.
